builds.name: Pixel Saber
builds.summary: An addressable-LED lightsaber that survives a duel. The clearest example on the map of two unrelated shelves turning into one object.

steps.why: The reference comes first. You cannot build to a frame you have not paused.
Soundboard pads are small and close together. Everything downstream is a joint that either holds or does not.
A blade is a long current draw. You size the cell before you buy the strip.
The board is flashed from the Arduino IDE. If you have done this for anything else, you have already done half of step eleven.
The hilt is the part people hold, and it is a prop before it is a circuit.
Greeblies, emitter and pommel, assembled dry, before anything is glued or wired.
Finish the hilt while it is still empty. The compressor you would have bought for a tank does this job.
Chassis, emitter insert and the tolerances that keep the blade from rattling.
Board, battery and speaker have to be held still inside a tube that gets hit.
Ignition, flicker and clash are three loops on a microcontroller.
Flash and configure on the bench. A setting changed after install costs a full teardown.
The build the other eleven steps were for.

builds.name: Model Train Channel
builds.summary: The stack behind a model railway channel: a modelling hobby and a video hobby that share almost nothing except patience, and have to be learned in a fixed order.

steps.why: Every purchase after this assumes the answer, which makes it the one decision here that is irreversible in practice.
Small and finished. People who get a train running reliably on a small layout stay; people who plan a huge one sell it.
Reliability is won or lost here, and poor trackwork causes more frustration in this hobby than anything else.
Bus, feeders and blocks, tested by actually running trains before a single scenic decision is made.
An address per locomotive, so a session has two trains in it and something to film.
Only now, and only over track you have proved. Ballast over unproven track is the classic irreversible mistake.
The single change that stops a layout photographing like a toy.
Miniatures need far more light than your eyes suggest, and at this scale depth of field is the whole problem.
Tripod, slider, and the onboard cab camera that gets a shot no other hobby can.
Recorded in the room, not repaired in the edit. No edit recovers a bad voiceover.
Cut the parts you enjoyed making. That is most of the difference between a build log and a video.
Thumbnail, title and cadence, which decide whether the other eleven steps were seen by anyone.

builds.name: Gunpla Contest Piece
builds.summary: A kit taken from snap-fit to cabinet-judged. Almost every step is a technique that transfers directly to armour, aircraft, miniatures and props.

steps.why: Grade literacy first. A Master Grade before your nub technique is reliable puts a permanent flaw on an expensive kit.
Cut proud of the part and shave the stub. Cutting flush whitens the plastic and that mark never comes out.
Cement, cure, sand. Erasing the fact the arm arrived as two halves, before anything is painted.
Priming is where every flaw you sanded past becomes visible, which is the point of doing it.
The cost and skill gate on gradients, modulation and any finish that has to be even.
Waterslides over gloss, then sealed. Silvering around a decal is what gives a rushed job away.
Chipping and soot applied on purpose, so the machine reads as one that has been used.
Faces, eyes and small details are brush work. The airbrush cannot do this part and never will.
Context, and in a contest roughly half of what the judge is actually looking at.
Online, the photograph is the entry. Nobody judging from a phone ever holds the model.
Cabinet judging against a standard nobody writes down. The fastest and least gentle feedback available.

builds.name: Solar Mesh Node
builds.summary: An off-grid LoRa node that ends up on a mast running on sunlight. No licence required, and the lowest entry cost of any build here.

steps.why: ESP32 for the web interface, nRF52 if the node has to survive weeks on one cell. The choice decides everything after it.
Headers, an antenna pigtail and a battery lead. Through hole is genuinely enough for this build.
Attach the antenna before the radio is ever powered. Keying into open air damages the chip, and this is the one hard safety rule here.
A real data cable, the serial driver and firmware. A charge-only cable is where most first attempts quietly stop.
Region and modem preset must match the whole mesh, and region is the legal envelope, not a preference.
A working node in your pocket that finds other people's nodes. Everything above this was setup.
Solar input, charge control and a battery sized for a week of cloud rather than a sunny afternoon.
Protected cells ship near their cutoff, which reads to a first-timer as a dead board rather than a flat one.
An enclosure that survives weather and can still be opened a year later without breaking.
On a mast, on a site somebody gave you permission for. That last part is the step people forget to plan.

builds.name: First HF Station
builds.summary: From listening on a dongle to talking to another continent. The licence is one of the very few genuinely hard prerequisites anywhere on this map.

steps.why: Listen first. A cheap dongle tells you whether the bands are alive where you live before you spend anything.
Technician, then General. General is the gate on the bands that reach other continents, and transmitting without it is not lawful.
Connectors and feedline. A badly soldered plug is the most common fault in a new station and the hardest to see.
A wire dipole in the garden beats an expensive vertical with no radials under it, every time.
An SWR meter and a multimeter turn a guess about the antenna into a measurement you can act on.
Transceiver, tuner, feedline and a desk. The first point at which the hobby needs a room rather than a pocket.
Why the same station reaches Japan at three in the morning and nothing at noon. Timing beats power.
FT8 gets a contact out of a signal no human ear can hear, which is what a modest antenna needs.
Carry a light station somewhere with a view. Portable operating is where this stops being a room and becomes a day out.

builds.name: Garage Kit Finish
builds.summary: The ladder from collecting finished figures to finishing an unpainted resin one yourself. A collector expects an assembly job and finds a refinishing job.

steps.why: The character comes first. Almost nobody finishes one of these for a show they were not already attached to.
Scale literacy, brand literacy, and knowing a recast when it arrives in the post.
Unpainted resin in a limited run. The point where the hobby changes from buying well to doing work.
Trim the casting seams and pour stubs, wet, because resin dust is the hazard nobody warns a collector about.
Brass rod through both halves of every joint. Resin is heavy and a butt joint fails while somebody is holding it.
An overnight soak and an ultrasonic clean. Mould release film is invisible and paint over it lifts weeks later.
Prime in a light mist coat then a heavier one. The first primer layer exposes flaws bare resin was hiding.
Bubbles that extend below the surface, so filling the top does not fix them. This is where the time actually goes.
The hardest step, and it happens before the hair is fitted because the hair blocks access permanently.
Macro, eye level and a plain backdrop. Shot from above, a finished figure looks like a toy on a desk.
The photograph is how everyone except your household will ever see six weeks of work.
